column1: What happens to a value's memory when its owning variable goes out of scope in Rust?
column2: The compiler inserts a synchronous call to `Drop::drop` at that exact lexical point, deterministically deallocating memory with no garbage collector or finalizer thread involved.

column1: What is 'move semantics by default' and what bug class does it eliminate at the type level?
column2: Assigning, passing, or returning an owner transfers ownership and statically invalidates the old binding; any later use is a compile error. This eliminates double-free, since you cannot free what you no longer own.

column1: State the borrow checker's 'aliasing XOR mutability' rule.
column2: At any point you may have either one mutable reference (`&mut T`) or any number of immutable references (`&T`) to the same data, but never both simultaneously.

column1: Why can lifetimes be described as 'compile-time variables over scopes' rather than runtime constructs?
column2: The compiler performs constraint-solving over lifetime annotations (explicit or inferred) to prove no reference outlives its referent's drop point, propagating validity across function and struct signatures without any runtime tracking.

column1: What hardware-level behaviors make naive concurrent reasoning ('A writes X, then B reads X') unreliable without explicit synchronization?
column2: CPUs reorder stores and loads for performance, maintain per-core caches that are not coherent by default, and execute instructions speculatively—so ordering must be enforced via explicit memory barriers.

column1: Define the `Send` and `Sync` marker traits and their formal relationship.
column2: `Send`: safe to transfer ownership of T to another thread. `Sync`: safe for multiple threads to hold `&T` simultaneously. Formally, T: Sync if and only if &T: Send.

column1: Why are data races undefined behavior but compile silently in C/C++, and how does Rust change this?
column2: C/C++ type systems have no concept of shared-data ownership across threads, so races are only caught dynamically (e.g., ThreadSanitizer) if an interleaving is exercised. Rust extends its single-threaded aliasing rules (no simultaneous &mut T and &T) with Send/Sync to make data races a compile-time type error.

column1: What is the key invariant of Rust's async model regarding when an `async fn`'s body begins executing?
column2: Calling an `async fn` immediately returns a Future without executing any body code; execution only proceeds when an executor polls that future (lazy evaluation).

column1: What are the two variants of `Poll<T>` and what does each signify?
column2: `Poll::Ready(T)` signals the future has completed with a value; `Poll::Pending` signals it cannot yet make progress, and it must have stored a cloned `Waker` from the `Context` before returning Pending.

column1: Why does OS-thread-per-connection concurrency fail to scale to tens of thousands of connections?
column2: Each OS thread requires a large stack (typically 2–8 MB on Linux) plus a kernel task control block, so 50,000 threads can consume hundreds of gigabytes of stack space before processing any application data.

column1: What is the fundamental invariant governing all Rust FFI interactions with C, and what does it define?
column2: The Application Binary Interface (ABI), which defines calling conventions, stack frame layout, register allocation for arguments, structure padding/alignment, and exception propagation—Rust must replicate these exactly for binary compatibility.

column1: On x86-64 System V (Linux/macOS), which registers hold the first six integer/pointer arguments in the C calling convention?
column2: RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, and R9 (with floating-point arguments passed in XMM0–XMM7).
